claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is in an as-cast or solution-treated state.
The initial alloy has a relatively coarse microstructure.
The initial alloy exhibits standard passive-film formation.
Significant cold working introduces a high dislocation density into the alloy.
Cold working followed by aging at approximately 400–500 °C for several hours induces nanoscale coherent precipitates.
The treatment produces a uniform dispersion of nanoscale coherent precipitates within the alloy matrix.
The fine precipitates hinder dislocation motion.
Precipitate-mediated hindrance of dislocation motion increases mechanical durability.
Precipitate-mediated hindrance of dislocation motion reduces room-temperature creep.
A uniform precipitate distribution promotes formation of a more stable and homogeneous passive film.
The more stable and homogeneous passive film enhances corrosion resistance.
Relative to the untreated condition, the treated alloy will have higher yield strength.
Relative to the untreated condition, the treated alloy will have a lower room-temperature creep deformation rate.
Relative to the untreated condition, the treated alloy will have a lower corrosion rate under accelerated testing.
The untreated alloy has lower mechanical durability, higher creep rates, and less robust corrosion resistance than the proposed treated alloy.
The beneficial effects occur only within an optimal window of cold-work extent, aging temperature, and aging duration.
Treatment outside the optimal window can produce an inappropriate precipitate size or distribution and negate or reverse the improvements.
